entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: A polite, indirect way to make a suggestion by asking whether the other person has considered an option.
entries.usage: Used with friends, coworkers and clients to give advice without sounding pushy, because the question leaves the decision to the other person. It is followed by a noun or an *-ing* form: *Have you thought about asking for a raise?* *Have you considered …* is a little more formal, and *Why don't you …* is more direct.
examples: "My back's been killing me for weeks." "**Have you thought about** seeing a physical therapist?"
**Have you thought about** renting out your basement? It could cover half the mortgage.
If the commute is wearing you down, **have you thought about** asking your boss if you can work from home twice a week?

drill.sentence: You're always complaining that your car costs too much to run. {{Have you thought about}} getting an e-bike for short trips?
drill.hint: a gentle suggestion: did this idea ever occur to you? (not *… considered* or *… tried*)

entries.related: *Have you considered …?* — same, more formal; *Why don't you …?* — more direct; *You might want to …* — a soft suggestion, not a question.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A tentative way to say that doing something could be useful, even though you are not sure it will help.
entries.usage: Common in advice at work and in daily life; *might* makes the suggestion soft and modest. It is followed by an *-ing* form or a noun: *It might be worth calling ahead*, *It might be worth a try*. *It's worth* + *-ing* sounds more confident.
entries.pattern: it might be worth + -ing / a try / a look
examples: The bridge is closed until Friday, so **it might be worth** leaving a little earlier tomorrow.
Before you buy a new laptop, **it might be worth** checking whether the battery can just be replaced.
"The doctor said it's probably nothing." "**It might be worth** getting a second opinion anyway."

drill.sentence: Flights are much cheaper midweek, so {{it might be worth}} moving the trip to a Tuesday.
drill.hint: this could pay off, said tentatively (not *it's …*, *… may …* or *… could …*)

mistake.wrong: It might be worth to call the hotel first.
mistake.right: It might be worth calling the hotel first.
mistake.why: *Worth* is followed by an *-ing* form or a noun, never a *to*-infinitive; German *es lohnt sich, … zu* leads learners to add *to*.

entries.related: *it's worth* + -ing — more confident; *it wouldn't hurt to* + verb — similar, casual; *it's not worth it* — the effort is too big for the gain.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A short reply that shows surprise or interest in what someone has just said; with a falling tone, it shows mild doubt.
entries.usage: With a rising tone, *Oh, really?* sounds interested and invites the speaker to say more. With a flat or falling tone, it sounds unconvinced or a little sarcastic, as if you doubt the claim. It is a reaction, not a real question, so the speaker usually just continues.
examples: "I grew up on a farm in Alaska." "**Oh, really?** What was that like?"
"I'll have the garage cleaned out by lunch." "**Oh, really?** You said that last weekend."
"They're closing the bakery on Main Street." "**Oh, really?** That's a shame. I loved their bagels."

drill.sentence: "Jenna's moving to Denver next month." "{{Oh, really}}? I had no idea. When did she decide?"
drill.hint: surprised and interested (two words, the first is *oh*; not *oh yeah* or *seriously*)

entries.related: *Really?* — the same, a bit sharper; *Oh yeah?* — casual, can sound challenging; *Seriously?* — stronger surprise or annoyance; *No way!* — strong, excited surprise.

entries.label: exclamation
entries.meaning: Said when you unexpectedly meet someone you know far from home, or find out that you and a new acquaintance know the same people.
entries.usage: A light, friendly exclamation, often *It's a small world!* or just *Small world!*, usually said with a laugh. It's common when traveling and when chatting with new people who turn out to share a friend, school or hometown. It is about people and coincidences, not about the size of a place.
examples: Wait, your cousin is Dana Ruiz? She was my roommate in college. **Small world!**
We ran into our next-door neighbors at a tiny café in Lisbon. **Small world!**
"My new boss used to coach my brother's soccer team." "Wow, **it's a small world**."

drill.sentence: I flew all the way to Tokyo and sat next to my old high school teacher on the subway. {{Small world}}, right?
drill.hint: people are more connected than you'd think (two words; not *what a coincidence*)

entries.related: *What a coincidence!* — for any surprising chance event; *What are the odds?* — stresses how unlikely it was; *Fancy meeting you here!* — joking greeting when you meet someone unexpectedly.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Said to someone who has had good luck or has something nice, usually with a little friendly envy.
entries.usage: A quick, warm reaction among friends and coworkers to news like a vacation, a day off or a great deal. With a flat tone it can sound envious or sarcastic, so the voice matters. It's also used ironically when someone gets an unpleasant job: *Lucky you, you get to clean the garage.*
examples: "I don't have to work on Friday." "**Lucky you!** I'm on call all weekend."
"My in-laws have a cabin on the lake, so we go up every August." "**Lucky you.**"
"I got picked for jury duty next week." "Ha, **lucky you**."

drill.sentence: "My company just switched to a four-day week." "{{Lucky you}}! We can't even leave early on Fridays."
drill.hint: I'm a bit jealous of your good fortune (two words; not *good for you*)

entries.related: *Good for you!* — happy for someone, without envy; *Must be nice* — openly envious, often sarcastic; *Some people have all the luck* — joking envy.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A sympathetic reply showing that you understand someone's situation is hard for them.
entries.usage: Said to friends, coworkers or acquaintances who tell you about a problem such as illness, money worries or a demanding job. It's kind but general, so people often add a question such as *How are you holding up?* *That must be hard* means the same; *That sucks* is much more casual.
examples: "My husband works nights, so we barely see each other." "**That must be tough.**"
"I'm taking care of my dad and working full-time." "Oh, **that must be tough**. How are you holding up?"
Moving to a new school in the middle of the year? **That must be tough** for your daughter.

drill.sentence: "I've been commuting three hours a day since the train line closed." "Wow, {{that must be tough}}."
drill.hint: sympathy: I imagine your situation is difficult (not *… hard*, *… rough*, *that sounds …* or *that sucks*)

entries.related: *That must be hard* — same; *That's rough* — casual; *That sucks* — very casual; *I'm sorry to hear that* — more formal and polite.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Tells someone that you have had the same experience or emotion, so you understand how they feel.
entries.usage: A friendly reply in casual conversation, usually to a small complaint about tiredness, stress or a bad day. It builds a connection, and people often follow it with a short story of their own. Use it only if you really have felt the same; otherwise *I can imagine* is more honest.
examples: "I think I need a vacation from my vacation." "Ha, **I know the feeling**."
"Every time I sit down, the baby wakes up." "Oh, **I know the feeling**. Mine's two now, and it's still the same."
Staring at a tax form for an hour and understanding nothing? Believe me, **I know the feeling**.

drill.sentence: "Mondays always hit me hard after a long weekend." "{{I know the feeling}}. I could barely get out of bed today."
drill.hint: I've had exactly the same experience (four words; not *tell me about it*)

entries.related: *Tell me about it* — I agree, it's annoying (about a shared problem); *Same here* — short and casual; *I can imagine* — sympathy without the same experience.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Reassures someone who is worried that the situation will turn out well.
entries.usage: Said to friends, family and coworkers before an exam, a trip, a medical test or a big meeting. It's kind but can sound dismissive if the person has a real problem, so it works best for ordinary nerves. Adding a reason makes it more convincing: *I'm sure it'll be fine; you've practiced a lot.*
examples: "I'm so nervous about my driving test tomorrow." "**I'm sure it'll be fine**. You've practiced for months."
The kids are staying with my parents for the first time, but **I'm sure it'll be fine**.
"What if the client hates the new design?" "**I'm sure it'll be fine**. They loved the first draft."

drill.sentence: "Our connecting flight leaves forty minutes after we land." "{{I'm sure it'll be fine}}. That airport's pretty small."
drill.hint: reassurance: things will go well (not *… okay* or *you'll …*)

entries.related: *It'll be fine* — same, shorter; *Don't worry* — plainer; *You'll do great* — reassurance about someone's performance.

entries.label: exclamation
entries.meaning: Expresses surprise, shock or excitement; a softer form of *oh my God*.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech, especially among people who avoid saying *God* casually, for example around kids or at work. It can be happy (*Oh my gosh, you're engaged!*) or upset (*Oh my gosh, I left the stove on!*). In texts it's often shortened to *OMG*.
examples: **Oh my gosh**, is that your baby? She's gotten so big!
**Oh my gosh**, I think I left my wallet at the restaurant.
"We're having twins." "**Oh my gosh!** Congratulations! When are they due?"

drill.sentence: {{Oh my gosh}}, look at all this snow! School's definitely canceled tomorrow.
drill.hint: a mild cry of surprise that avoids saying *God* (not *oh my goodness* or *wow*)

entries.related: *Oh my goodness* — same, a bit more old-fashioned; *Oh my God* — stronger, avoided by some speakers; *Wow* — neutral surprise or admiration.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Reacts to something very surprising, unusual or hard to believe; it does not mean that anyone is mentally ill.
entries.usage: One of the most common reactions in casual American conversation, used with friends and coworkers about news, coincidences or prices. Depending on the tone, it can sound impressed, shocked or disapproving. In emails or formal settings, *That's surprising* or *That's remarkable* fits better.
examples: "Rent for a one-bedroom here is three thousand a month." "**That's crazy.**"
My parents met on a train and got married two weeks later. **That's crazy**, right?
Forty dollars to park downtown for two hours? **That's crazy**.

drill.sentence: "My neighbor is ninety-four and still goes skiing every winter." "{{That's crazy}}! My knees hurt just thinking about it."
drill.hint: casual reaction: wow, hard to believe (two words; not *… amazing*, *… insane*, *… wild* or *no way*)

entries.related: *That's insane* — stronger, very casual; *That's wild* — casual, a little younger-sounding; *No way!* — I can't believe it; *That's amazing* — clearly positive.

entries.label: exclamation
entries.meaning: Expresses relief that something good happened or that something bad didn't happen.
entries.usage: Used in conversation and informal messages, alone or before a clause: *Thank goodness you're here.* It's a softer form of *thank God*, so it suits work, school and family settings. *Thank goodness for* + noun expresses thanks for a thing or person: *Thank goodness for coffee.*
examples: **Thank goodness** you called. I was about to leave without the tickets.
"The test results came back normal." "Oh, **thank goodness**. I was so worried."
The power was out for two days. **Thank goodness for** our neighbor's generator.

drill.sentence: {{Thank goodness}} it stopped raining before the ceremony. The whole wedding was outdoors.
drill.hint: what a relief that (the soft form without *God*; not *luckily* or *thankfully*)

entries.related: *Thank God* — stronger, avoided by some speakers; *thankfully* — adverb, also used in writing; *Phew!* — a sound of relief.

entries.label: exclamation
entries.meaning: Praise for someone's success or good action; it means *well done!*
entries.usage: Warm and casual: parents say it to kids, coaches to players, friends and coworkers to each other. The same pattern works with other verbs: *Way to stay calm out there!* Said flatly after a mistake, it's sarcastic: *Way to go, now we're locked out.*
examples: "I passed the bar exam!" "**Way to go!** We have to celebrate this weekend."
**Way to go**, Emma! That was your best swim all season.
"I just spilled coffee on the new couch." "Great. **Way to go**."

drill.sentence: You finished your first half marathon? {{Way to go}}! I'm so proud of you.
drill.hint: well done! (three words; not *good for you* or *nice work*)

entries.related: *Good job* / *Nice work* — similar praise; *Good for you* — happy about someone's choice or luck; *Keep it up* — encourages someone to continue.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Encourages someone to continue doing something well, usually right after praising their progress.
entries.usage: Common from teachers, coaches, managers and parents, usually after a compliment: *Great job on the report, keep it up!* It sounds supportive but a little like a mentor speaking, so it's less natural to say to your boss. *Keep up the good work* is a slightly longer, more formal version.
examples: Your grades have really improved this semester. **Keep it up!**
"I've lost ten pounds since January." "That's great! **Keep it up**."
Sales were up again this quarter, everyone, so let's **keep it up**.

drill.sentence: You've gone to the gym four times a week for a whole month? Nice! {{Keep it up}}.
drill.hint: don't stop now, continue like this (three words; not *… going* or *… at it*)

entries.related: *Keep up the good work* — slightly more formal; *Keep going* — don't stop, often in the middle of an effort; *Way to go* — praise for a finished success.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Praises someone's positive, brave or determined attitude, especially after a setback.
entries.usage: Said to a friend, teammate or child who decides to try again or stays cheerful in a bad situation. It sounds encouraging, a bit like a coach or a parent; with a flat tone it can be ironic. It praises an attitude, not a result, so use *nice job* for a success.
examples: "I didn't get the job, but I'm applying for three more this week." "**That's the spirit!**"
"It's pouring, but we're still having the picnic. We'll just eat in the car." "Ha, **that's the spirit**."
When my daughter said she'd practice the piano piece until she got it right, I told her, "**That's the spirit.**"

drill.sentence: "My first loaf of bread was a disaster, but I'm baking another one tonight." "{{That's the spirit}}!"
drill.hint: I love that positive attitude (three words, with *the*; not *good for you*)

entries.related: *Good for you* — happy about someone's choice; *That's more like it* — finally, an improvement; *Keep it up* — continue doing well.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Tells someone to relax, rest or calm down; it is also a casual way to say goodbye.
entries.usage: As advice, it's said to someone who is overworking, sick or upset: *Take it easy this weekend.* Said to an angry person, it can sound dismissive, like *calm down*. As a goodbye between friends and coworkers it's very casual, like *see you*.
examples: You just got over the flu, so **take it easy** this weekend.
"All right, I'm heading out." "**Take it easy**, man. See you Monday."
**Take it easy!** It was an accident. He didn't mean to scratch your car.

drill.sentence: The doctor said I can go back to work, but I should {{take it easy}} for a couple of weeks.
drill.hint: relax and not do too much (not *… slow*, *rest up* or *slow down*)

entries.related: *take it easy on someone* — don't be too hard on them; *calm down* — more direct, can annoy; *take care* — a warmer goodbye.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Tells someone in a hard situation that you will support them and that they can count on you.
entries.usage: Said to close friends, partners and family during illness, grief, a breakup or a crisis. It's warm and serious, so it can sound too heavy for small problems or with people you barely know. People often add something concrete: *I'm here for you if you need anything.*
examples: I know the divorce has been hard. Just remember **I'm here for you**, okay?
"I don't even know who to talk to anymore." "You can talk to me. **I'm here for you**."
Whatever happens with the surgery, **we're here for you**, Mom.

drill.sentence: Call me anytime, day or night. {{I'm here for you}}.
drill.hint: I'll support you, whatever you need (four words; not *I've got your back* or *I've got you*)

entries.related: *I've got your back* — I'll defend or protect you, more casual; *Let me know if you need anything* — a lighter offer of help.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Said to someone who is sick, meaning *I hope you get well soon*.
entries.usage: The usual way Americans wish a sick friend, coworker or child a quick recovery, often as *Feel better soon!* or *Hope you feel better!* It fits short illnesses like a cold or the flu; for a serious illness, people usually say more. *Get well soon* means the same and is very common on cards.
examples: "I'm staying home today with a fever." "Oh no. **Feel better!**"
Sorry you missed the party last night. **Hope you feel better** soon!
She texted her coworker: "Don't worry about the meeting. Just rest and **feel better**."

drill.sentence: Sorry to hear you've got strep throat. Drink lots of fluids and {{feel better}} soon!
drill.hint: a wish for a quick recovery (two words; not *get well* or *get …*)

entries.related: *Get well soon* — same, also on cards; *Hope you're feeling better* — said when the person may already be recovering; *Take care of yourself* — warmer, more general.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A standard, polite expression of sympathy to someone whose family member, friend or pet has died.
entries.usage: Said at funerals, in cards, and when a coworker or acquaintance tells you the news. It's respectful but a bit formulaic, so close friends often add something personal, such as a memory of the person. *I'm so sorry* alone is also fine and sounds warm.
examples: "My grandmother passed away last week." "Oh, **I'm so sorry for your loss**."
At the funeral, dozens of people shook his hand and said, "**I'm sorry for your loss**."
I just heard about your dad. **I'm very sorry for your loss**, Linda.

drill.sentence: Mrs. Carter, I was so sad to hear about your husband. {{I'm sorry for your loss}}.
drill.hint: standard sympathy after a death (not *my condolences*)

entries.related: *My condolences* — more formal, often written; *My thoughts are with you* — formal; *I'm so sorry to hear about* + person — warmer and more personal.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: An informal way to ask why someone is doing something or what it is for.
entries.usage: Short and direct, used with family, friends and coworkers after a request or an announcement. Depending on the tone, it sounds curious or suspicious, so with your boss *Can I ask what it's for?* is safer. In the longer form, *what* comes first and *for* at the end: *What did you do that for?*
examples: "Can you lend me fifty bucks until Friday?" "**What for?**"
**What** did you buy a second blender **for**? We never even use the first one.
"Mom, I need poster board and glue." "**What for?**" "A school project that's due tomorrow."

drill.sentence: "I need to leave work early tomorrow." "Oh? {{What for}}?" "A dentist appointment."
drill.hint: asking the purpose (two words; not *how come* or *why's that*)

entries.related: *Why?* — neutral; *How come?* — casual, asks for the reason or cause; *Why's that?* — friendlier, shows interest.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Asks someone to give examples of something they have just mentioned in general terms.
entries.usage: Casual and common when someone's statement is vague, such as *We should do something fun.* It can sound genuinely curious or a bit challenging, as if you doubt there are any good examples. In a meeting, *Could you give an example?* is more polite.
examples: "We should do something different for Mom's birthday this year." "**Like what?**"
"There are lots of easy ways to cut our grocery bill." "Okay, **like what**?"
"The new phone has tons of new features." "**Like what?** It looks exactly like the old one."

drill.sentence: "There's so much to do in Chicago in the winter." "Really? {{Like what}}? Isn't it freezing?"
drill.hint: give me some examples (two words; not *such as* or *for example*)

entries.related: *For example?* — similar, a bit more neutral; *Such as?* — more formal; *What do you mean?* — asks for an explanation, not examples.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Asks someone to explain the reason for what they have just said.
entries.usage: A natural follow-up question in conversation, softer and friendlier than a bare *Why?* It shows interest rather than disagreement, so it works well with coworkers and new acquaintances. *Why's that* is the contraction of *why is that*.
examples: "I'd never live in a big city again." "Oh, **why's that**?"
"I really don't like working in an open office." "**Why's that?**" "I can't hear myself think."
"We're switching to a different bank next month." "Really? **Why's that**?"

drill.sentence: "I stopped drinking coffee after lunch." "Oh, {{why's that}}?" "I couldn't fall asleep at night."
drill.hint: asking the reason (two words; not *how come* or *what for*)

entries.related: *How come?* — casual, same meaning; *What for?* — asks about the purpose; *Why?* — shorter, can sound blunt.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Asks someone to continue speaking, showing that you are listening and interested.
entries.usage: Said when someone pauses, hesitates or has been interrupted, often as *Go on, I'm listening.* It sounds patient and encouraging with friends, family and colleagues. It can also push someone who is unsure whether to tell you something: *Go on, tell me.*
examples: "So I opened the door, and guess who was standing there…" "Who? **Go on!**"
"I'm not sure I should tell you this." "Well, now you have to. **Go on**."
Sorry, I cut you off. **Go on**, what happened after that?

drill.sentence: "There's something I've been meaning to tell you, but…" "It's okay. {{Go on}}. I'm listening."
drill.hint: continue talking (two words; not *keep going* or *go ahead*)

entries.related: *Keep going* — same, often when someone stops halfway; *And then?* — asks for the next part of a story; *Shoot* — go ahead, ask or tell me.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: An informal reply that means *go ahead, ask or tell me*, used after someone says they have a question or something to say.
entries.usage: The typical answer to *Can I ask you something?* among friends and coworkers. It sounds relaxed and friendly, but too casual for formal situations. Don't confuse it with *Shoot!* as a mild curse when something goes wrong: *Shoot, I forgot my keys.*
examples: "Can I ask you something kind of personal?" "Sure, **shoot**."
"I've got a quick question about the schedule for Saturday." "**Shoot.**"
"Hey, got a minute? I need your advice on something." "Yeah, **shoot**."

drill.sentence: "I have a weird question about your neighbor's dog." "Okay, {{shoot}}."
drill.hint: one casual word: I'm ready for your question (not *fire away*)

entries.related: *Fire away* — same, a bit more playful; *Go ahead* — neutral; *I'm all ears* — I'm eager to listen.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Says that you are ready and eager to listen to what someone wants to tell you.
entries.usage: Used playfully when someone has news, a story or an idea, with friends and in relaxed meetings. It usually sounds keen and curious. With a flat tone, it can be a challenge, as if you doubt anyone has a better answer: *If you have a better plan, I'm all ears.*
examples: "I think I know how to fix the leak under the sink." "**I'm all ears.**"
"Want to hear what happened on my date last night?" "Absolutely. **I'm all ears**."
If anyone has a cheaper way to get six people to Florida, **I'm all ears**.

drill.sentence: You've got gossip about the new neighbors? Sit down, {{I'm all ears}}.
drill.hint: I'm ready and eager to hear it; three words (not *I'm listening* or *tell me everything*)

entries.related: *I'm listening* — neutral; *Go on* — continue, I'm listening; *Tell me everything* — eager, about news or gossip.

entries.label: polite request
entries.meaning: A very polite way to ask someone to do something, especially when the request is a real favor.
entries.usage: *Possibly* softens the request, as if you know it may be inconvenient. It suits neighbors, colleagues and service staff; with close friends it can sound overly formal, and with an annoyed tone it turns sarcastic: *Could you possibly be any louder?* It is followed by the base form of a verb.
examples: **Could you possibly** feed our cat this weekend? We'll be back Sunday night.
Sorry to bother you, but **could you possibly** turn the music down a little? The baby's asleep.
**Could you possibly** look over my slides before the meeting with the client?

drill.sentence: I know it's short notice, but {{could you possibly}} pick me up from the airport on Friday?
drill.hint: a very polite request with a softening adverb (not *would you mind* or *… maybe*)

entries.related: *Could you …?* — polite, everyday; *Would you mind* + -ing — equally polite; *Would you be able to …?* — polite, asks about time or ability.

entries.label: polite request
entries.meaning: A polite request that asks whether someone has the time or ability to do something, instead of asking them directly.
entries.usage: Very common in work emails, phone calls and requests to service providers, landlords or neighbors. It's polite without sounding stiff, and it gives the other person an easy way to say no. Among close friends it can sound a bit formal; *Could you …?* or *Can you …?* is more usual there.
entries.pattern: Would you be able to + base verb?
examples: **Would you be able to** watch the kids for an hour on Saturday morning?
Hi, this is Mark in 4B. **Would you be able to** come by and look at the heater?
**Would you be able to** move our call to Thursday afternoon? Something came up.

drill.sentence: Hi, I'm calling about my order. {{Would you be able to}} deliver it before noon tomorrow?
drill.hint: polite: do you have the time or means to …? (not *could you*, *can you* or *is it possible to*)

entries.related: *Could you …?* — shorter, everyday; *Could you possibly …?* — very polite, for a bigger favor; *Would you mind* + -ing — polite, asks whether it bothers them.

entries.term: if it's not too much trouble
entries.label: softener
entries.meaning: Makes a request softer by saying that you want it only if it is easy for the other person.
entries.usage: Added at the end or the beginning of a request to hosts, neighbors, coworkers or service staff. It sounds considerate, and a little formal among close friends. *If it's no trouble* means the same and is slightly shorter.
examples: Could you drop this package at the post office on your way, **if it's not too much trouble**?
**If it's not too much trouble**, I'd love a copy of that lasagna recipe.
Could I get the dressing on the side, **if it's not too much trouble**?

drill.sentence: {{If it's not too much trouble}}, could you water my tomatoes while I'm away?
drill.hint: only if it's easy for you; six words (not the shorter *… no …* version)

entries.related: *if it's no trouble* — same, shorter; *if you don't mind* — similar, more common; *if you get a chance* — no hurry, only when convenient.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Asks whether someone has time at a certain moment, usually just before an invitation or a request.
entries.usage: Common with friends and coworkers, followed by a time: *Are you free Saturday night?* It signals that an invitation or request is coming, so people often answer cautiously: *Why, what's up?* In American English the day often comes without *on*: *Are you free Friday?*
entries.pattern: Are you free + time (+ for + noun / to + verb)?
examples: **Are you free** Saturday night? A few of us are going bowling.
**Are you free** for a quick call at three? I want to run something by you.
"**Are you free** this weekend?" "Depends. Is this about helping you move?"

drill.sentence: {{Are you free}} Sunday afternoon? We're grilling in the backyard and would love to have you.
drill.hint: do you have time then? (not *… available*, *… around* or *… busy*)

entries.related: *Are you available …?* — more formal, for work; *Are you around …?* — casual: are you in town; *Are you busy?* — asked before a request, often for right now.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A polite way to let someone go before you, for example through a door, into an elevator or in a line.
entries.usage: Said with a small gesture toward the door or the line, to strangers and colleagues alike; the other person usually just says *Thanks*. If both people say it at once, the usual joke is *No, after you!*
examples: He held the door open for the woman with the stroller and said, "**After you**."
"Do you want to get on first?" "No, please, **after you**."
"Go ahead, you were here first." "Oh no, **after you**. I'm still deciding."

drill.sentence: We reached the elevator at the same time, so I stepped aside and said, "{{After you}}."
drill.hint: please go first (two words; not *go ahead*)

entries.related: *Go ahead* — more casual, also gives permission; *Ladies first* — old-fashioned; *Be my guest* — go ahead, take it or do it.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Encourages someone to do something they want to do, especially something a little risky or new.
entries.usage: Said to friends, family and coworkers who are unsure about a plan: *If you want the job, go for it!* It sounds positive and supportive. It's also a quick way to give permission, as in *Sure, go for it* when someone asks for the last slice of pizza.
examples: "I'm thinking about quitting my job to open a bakery." "If you really want it, **go for it**."
"Mind if I grab the last slice of pizza?" "**Go for it.** I'm stuffed."
She'd always wanted to learn to surf, so at forty she finally **went for it**.

drill.sentence: "Should I ask her out? I'm scared she'll say no." "You'll never know unless you try. {{Go for it}}!"
drill.hint: do it, take the chance (three words; not *just do it*)

entries.related: *Go ahead* — permission, less enthusiastic; *Give it a shot* — try it, even if you might fail; *Why not?* — casual agreement.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Said by a host to a guest: relax and feel free to act as if this were your own home.
entries.usage: A warm welcome when a guest arrives or is staying over, often with practical details about drinks, towels or the TV. It invites the guest to sit down, help themselves and relax. Said sarcastically, it criticizes someone who acts too freely in your space.
examples: Our cousins arrived late Friday night, and Mom told them to **make themselves at home**.
"Thanks for letting me stay." "Of course! **Make yourself at home**. The fridge is all yours."
My roommate's boyfriend put his feet on our table and ate my leftovers. **Make yourself at home**, I guess.

drill.sentence: Welcome! Put your bags in the guest room, grab a drink, and {{make yourself at home}}.
drill.hint: relax and act as if this house were yours (not *… comfortable*)

mistake.wrong: Come in and feel like at home!
mistake.right: Come in and make yourself at home!
mistake.why: German *Fühl dich wie zu Hause* does not translate word for word; the English set phrase is *make yourself at home*.

entries.related: *Help yourself* — take any food or drink you want; *Make yourself comfortable* — sit down and relax; *Mi casa es su casa* — joking, borrowed from Spanish.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you don't feel like doing something right now, because of how you feel at the moment.
entries.usage: Common with friends, family and partners to turn down an activity, a food or a topic. It takes *for* + noun or *to* + verb: *I'm not in the mood for pizza*, *I'm not in the mood to argue.* It's honest but can sound grumpy, so people soften it with *really* or *tonight*.
entries.pattern: not in the mood + for + noun / to + verb
examples: "Want to go to Jake's party tonight?" "Honestly, **I'm not in the mood**. I just want to stay in."
**I'm not in the mood for** Mexican food again. We had it twice this week.
Don't tease your brother right now. **He's not in the mood**.

drill.sentence: Sorry, I had a terrible day at work, and {{I'm not in the mood}} to talk about it right now.
drill.hint: it doesn't suit how I feel at the moment (not *I don't want*)

mistake.wrong: I have no lust to go out tonight.
mistake.right: I'm not in the mood to go out tonight.
mistake.why: German *Lust* is a false friend: English *lust* means strong sexual desire, so use *not in the mood* or *don't feel like*.

entries.related: *I don't feel like it* — very similar; *I'm not up for it* — I don't have the energy; *I'm in the mood for* + noun — I'd like to have or do it now.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Tells someone that you are busy or that the moment is wrong, so they should talk to you later.
entries.usage: A polite but firm way to put off a conversation, a visitor or a call, usually with an apology and an offer to talk later. It's common on the phone and when someone stops by your desk or your door. *Now isn't a good time* and *This isn't a good time* mean the same.
examples: "Hey, got a minute?" "Sorry, **now's not a good time**. Can we talk after lunch?"
I answered the phone in the middle of dinner and told my cousin, "**Now's not a good time**."
If **now's not a good time**, I can come back tomorrow morning.

drill.sentence: "Can we talk about the vacation plans?" "Sorry, honey, {{now's not a good time}}. I'm about to get on a work call."
drill.hint: I'm busy at this moment (not *this isn't …* or *it's not …*)

entries.related: *I'm in the middle of something* — I'm busy with a task; *Can I call you back?* — polite delay on the phone; *Is this a good time?* — the question before you start talking.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Tells someone that you will deal with a task or problem, so they don't need to worry about it.
entries.usage: Used at home and at work to take responsibility for something: *Leave the dishes, I'll take care of it.* It sounds reliable and reassuring. When the check comes in a restaurant, *I'll take care of it* can also mean that you'll pay.
examples: "The smoke alarm keeps beeping." "Don't worry, **I'll take care of it** after work."
"Who's going to call the insurance company?" "**I'll take care of it**."
When the check came, my uncle grabbed it and said, "**I'll take care of it**."

drill.sentence: "Someone needs to call the cable company about the internet." "{{I'll take care of it}}. I'm home tomorrow anyway."
drill.hint: the task is mine now, no need to worry (not *… handle it*, *… deal with it* or *I've got it*)

entries.related: *I'll handle it* — same, a bit more businesslike; *I've got it* — casual; *Consider it done* — eager reply to a request.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: An eager, confident reply to a request: you will certainly do it, and quickly.
entries.usage: Said to a boss, colleague, friend or family member who asks for something; it sounds keen and a little playful. It's best for small, easy tasks, because for a big job it can sound like an empty promise. A shorter version is simply *Done!*
examples: "Could you book a table for Friday night?" "**Consider it done.**"
"Grab me a coffee if you're going downstairs?" "**Consider it done**. Oat milk, right?"
"I need these copies by ten." "**Consider it done**," the new intern said, already walking to the printer.

drill.sentence: "Could you send everyone the address for Saturday's party?" "{{Consider it done}}. I'll text the group right now."
drill.hint: eager: as good as finished already (three words; not *you got it* or *I'm on it*)

entries.related: *You got it* — casual, same idea; *Will do* — short and neutral; *I'll take care of it* — I'll deal with the problem.

entries.label: polite refusal
entries.meaning: Politely refuses an offer of help by saying that you can do something by yourself.
entries.usage: A common reply when someone offers to carry something, help with a task or lend money: *Thanks, but I can manage.* It sounds independent and polite; said sharply, it can sound proud or irritated. *I've got it* is more casual.
examples: "Want me to carry one of those boxes?" "Thanks, but **I can manage**."
My neighbor's eighty-five and won't let anyone carry her groceries. "**I can manage**," she always says.
"If money's tight this month, I can lend you some." "That's sweet, but **I can manage**."

drill.sentence: "Let me help you with that suitcase." "Thanks, but {{I can manage}}. It's lighter than it looks."
drill.hint: polite refusal: you're able to do it alone (three words; not *I've got it* or *I'm all good*)

entries.related: *I've got it* — casual, same meaning; *I'm good, thanks* — casual refusal of an offer; *I could use a hand* — the opposite: I'd like some help.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Asks someone not to make a special effort for you, for example when they offer to cook or prepare something.
entries.usage: A polite reply to a host or friend who offers to cook, set something up or change their plans for you. It's partly sincere and partly a social ritual, so hosts often go ahead anyway. *Please don't go to too much trouble* and *Don't go out of your way* are common variants.
examples: "I'll make you something to eat." "Oh, **don't go to any trouble**. A sandwich is fine."
We're only staying one night, so **don't go to any trouble** with the guest room.
"I could bake a cake for your birthday." "Please **don't go to any trouble**. Just come!"

drill.sentence: "I'll make a fresh pot of coffee." "Oh, {{don't go to any trouble}}. Water's fine."
drill.hint: no special effort for me, please (not *… bother* or *… out of your way*)

entries.related: *Don't bother* — shorter, can sound less warm; *Don't go out of your way* — don't make an extra effort; *You shouldn't have* — thanks after someone did make the effort.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A polite thank-you for an offer, very often said just before you decline it.
entries.usage: Works with friends, coworkers and salespeople: *Thanks for the offer, but I'm all set.* It keeps a refusal friendly, so a *but* usually follows. It can also leave the door open: *Thanks for the offer; let me think about it.*
examples: "Want a ride home?" "**Thanks for the offer**, but I'll walk. It's a nice night."
**Thanks for the offer**, but we already found a babysitter for Friday.
"I could help you paint this weekend." "**Thanks for the offer**! Let me check with Ben first."

drill.sentence: "You can borrow my truck for the move if you want." "{{Thanks for the offer}}, but my brother's lending me his van."
drill.hint: I appreciate you suggesting it, before saying no (four words; not *that's kind of you*)

entries.related: *That's very kind of you* — warmer, praises the person; *Thanks, but no thanks* — a firm, slightly rude refusal; *I appreciate it* — neutral thanks.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Accepts something after first refusing it, because the other person keeps offering.
entries.usage: Part of a polite ritual: someone offers, you say no, they insist, and you give in with *Well, if you insist.* It's often said with a smile when you secretly wanted it, like another piece of cake. With a flat tone, it shows that you disagree but won't argue.
examples: "Have another slice. Really, there's plenty." "Well, **if you insist**."
"No, dinner's on me tonight." "Okay, **if you insist**. Next time's my treat."
"We're taking my car, and that's final." "Fine, **if you insist**, but you're paying for parking."

drill.sentence: "Please, let us pay for the taxi." "No, no, that's okay." "We want to!" "Well, {{if you insist}}."
drill.hint: okay, since you keep offering (not *if you say so*)

entries.related: *If you say so* — I doubt it, but I won't argue; *I insist* — the offer that comes before it; *Don't mind if I do* — playful acceptance.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Says firmly but kindly that you really want to do something for someone, such as pay or help, and won't accept a refusal.
entries.usage: A reply to someone who politely refuses your offer: *No, I insist, it's my treat.* It's friendly but firm, used with guests, friends and colleagues. With a verb, use *insist on* + *-ing*: *I insist on paying.*
examples: "You don't have to drive me home." "**I insist**. It's dark, and it's pouring."
No, you take the bigger bedroom. **I insist**; you're the one working from home.
"Really, we can take a cab from the airport." "Absolutely not. **I insist on** picking you up."

drill.sentence: "You don't need to buy my coffee." "Nope, {{I insist}}. You helped me move last week."
drill.hint: I really want to, don't argue (two words; not *my treat*)

mistake.wrong: I insist to pay for dinner.
mistake.right: I insist on paying for dinner.

entries.related: *It's on me* — I'm paying; *my treat* — I'm paying, as a gift; *if you insist* — the reply that accepts.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A short way to admit that you were wrong about something small and to say sorry.
entries.usage: Used for minor errors such as a wrong name, time or seat, in conversation and quick emails: *My mistake, the meeting is at two.* It sounds polite and matter-of-fact. *My bad* is the slangy version, too casual for work emails; a serious error needs a fuller apology.
examples: "I'm actually Kate, not Katie." "Oh, **my mistake**. Nice to meet you, Kate."
**My mistake**, everyone: the dinner reservation is for seven thirty, not seven.
"You gave me change for a twenty, but I gave you a fifty." "Oh, **my mistake**. Here you go."

drill.sentence: "Excuse me, I think you're in my seat." "Oh, {{my mistake}}. I'm one row back."
drill.hint: I was wrong, sorry (two words; not *my bad* or *my fault*)

entries.related: *My bad* — slang, very casual; *My fault* — I'm to blame; *I stand corrected* — formal, accepts that you were wrong.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: An apology for making someone wait for you, for example when you arrive late or serve them slowly.
entries.usage: Said by doctors, receptionists, servers and hosts, and by anyone arriving late to a meeting or a call. It's polite and neutral; *Sorry for the wait* is a shorter, more casual version. In emails, *Sorry for the delay* or *Sorry for the late reply* is more common.
examples: **Sorry to keep you waiting**, Mr. Jensen. The doctor will see you now.
**Sorry to keep you waiting**! The traffic on the bridge was terrible.
Thanks for holding, and **sorry to keep you waiting**. How can I help you today?

drill.sentence: {{Sorry to keep you waiting}}. Your table's ready now, so just follow me.
drill.hint: apology for the delay; five words (not *… for the wait*, *… for keeping …* or *… make you wait*)

entries.related: *Sorry for the wait* — shorter, casual; *Thanks for your patience* — thanks instead of an apology; *Sorry I'm late* — when you arrive late yourself.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A promise, after an apology, that you will not make the same mistake again.
entries.usage: Said to a boss, teacher, partner or customer after apologizing for being late, forgetting something or making an error. It's a standard part of a serious apology at work; among friends it sounds a bit formal. It sounds empty if you have to say it often.
examples: I'm really sorry I missed the deadline. **It won't happen again**.
"You were supposed to be home by eleven." "I know, Dad. I'm sorry. **It won't happen again**."
The airline apologized for losing our luggage and promised **it wouldn't happen again**.

drill.sentence: I'm so sorry I forgot to pick you up from practice. {{It won't happen again}}, I promise.
drill.hint: I'll never repeat this mistake (not *I'll make it up to you*)

entries.related: *I'll make it up to you* — I'll do something nice to fix it; *Lesson learned* — I understand my mistake; *My bad* — casual apology for a small error.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Thanks someone who tried to help or offered something, even though it didn't work out or you didn't need it.
entries.usage: Said after a failed attempt to help, for example when a stranger can't give directions or a store doesn't have your size. It's polite and friendly; with a sigh it can also show disappointment. It also politely declines an offer you don't need: *No, I'm okay, thanks anyway.*
examples: "Sorry, I'm not from around here either." "No problem, **thanks anyway**."
"We're out of that size, but we might get more next week." "Okay, **thanks anyway**."
My cousin can't lend us his tent after all, but tell him **thanks anyway**.

drill.sentence: "Sorry, I looked everywhere, but I couldn't find your charger." "That's okay. {{Thanks anyway}}."
drill.hint: I appreciate the effort, even though it didn't work (two words; not *… for trying*)

entries.related: *Thanks for trying* — same, stresses the effort; *Thanks for the offer* — usually before declining; *No worries* — it's fine, don't feel bad.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A warm, polite way to thank someone for a gift or favor, suggesting that it was more than you expected.
entries.usage: Said when you receive a present, flowers or an unexpected kindness, usually followed by *thank you*. It doesn't mean the person did something wrong; it's a modest, pleased reaction. Said in a flat tone about an ugly or strange gift, it's a well-known joke.
examples: "Happy birthday! I got you a little something." "Oh, **you shouldn't have**! Thank you."
**You shouldn't have** gone to all this trouble. Everything looks amazing.
When her students gave her flowers on the last day of school, the teacher said, "Oh, **you shouldn't have**."

drill.sentence: "We brought you a bottle of wine for the new place." "Aw, {{you shouldn't have}}! Come in, come in."
drill.hint: polite thanks for a gift, phrased like a mild scolding (three words)

entries.related: *That's so sweet of you* — warm thanks; *You didn't have to do that* — similar, more literal; *Thank you so much* — plain thanks.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A polite way to thank someone for an offer, a compliment or help.
entries.usage: Common with neighbors, colleagues, older people and strangers; it's warmer and a little more formal than *thanks*. It can come before accepting or declining: *That's very kind of you, but I'm fine.* After a compliment, people often say *That's very kind of you to say.*
entries.pattern: That's very kind of you (to + verb)
examples: "I can drop you off at the station on my way." "**That's very kind of you**, thank you."
"Your speech at the wedding was wonderful." "Oh, **that's very kind of you** to say."
"**That's very kind of you**, but I've already eaten," she said when the neighbor offered her some soup.

drill.sentence: "Let me hold the umbrella over you until your bus comes." "Oh, {{that's very kind of you}}."
drill.hint: warm, polite thanks that praises the person (not *… nice of you* or *… sweet of you*)

mistake.why: After *kind / nice / sweet*, English uses *of* + person; German *von* leads learners to say *from*.

entries.related: *That's so nice of you* — same, more casual; *That's sweet of you* — warm, informal; *I appreciate it* — neutral thanks.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Thanks someone for giving you information, especially news, a warning or a change of plans.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, texts and work emails as a reply to updates like *I'll be ten minutes late.* It's polite and neutral, and it closes the topic without further comment. *Thanks for the heads-up* is a more casual version, used mainly for warnings.
examples: "The pool's closed for repairs until Monday." "Oh, **thanks for letting me know**."
"I'm running about fifteen minutes late." "No worries, **thanks for letting me know**."
**Thanks for letting us know** about the leak. We'll send someone tomorrow morning.

drill.sentence: "Mom's running late, so dinner's at eight now." "Okay, {{thanks for letting me know}}."
drill.hint: I appreciate the information (not *… for the heads-up* or *… for the update*)

entries.related: *Thanks for the heads-up* — casual, for warnings; *Good to know* — neutral: the information is useful; *Thanks for the update* — common in work emails.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A warm reply to *thank you*, meaning that you were happy to help.
entries.usage: Warmer and a little more polite than *you're welcome*, so it's very common in hotels, restaurants and shops, but friends use it too. It suggests the help was no burden at all. *It was my pleasure* is the full form.
examples: "Thanks for watering my plants while I was away." "**My pleasure**. They're doing great."
"Thank you for dinner. It was delicious." "**My pleasure**. Come again anytime."
"Thank you so much," I said, and the hotel clerk smiled: "**My pleasure**. Enjoy your stay."

drill.sentence: "Thank you so much for helping me with my cover letter." "{{My pleasure}}! Good luck with the interview."
drill.hint: warm: I enjoyed helping you; two words (not *you're welcome*, *no problem*, *no worries* or *of course*)

entries.related: *You're welcome* — standard; *Don't mention it* — modest: it was nothing; *Anytime* — casual: I'd do it again.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A modest reply to *thank you*, meaning that the help was too small to need thanks.
entries.usage: Friendly and modest, used with friends, neighbors and coworkers after a small favor. It plays the favor down, unlike *my pleasure*, which stresses that you enjoyed helping. It doesn't literally ask the person to keep quiet about it.
examples: "Thanks for jump-starting my car." "**Don't mention it**. It happens to everyone."
"I owe you big time for covering my shift." "**Don't mention it**. You'd do the same for me."
When I thanked our neighbor for shoveling our driveway, he just waved and said, "**Don't mention it**."

drill.sentence: "Thanks for lending me your ladder." "Oh, {{don't mention it}}. Keep it as long as you need."
drill.hint: modest: the favor was too small to thank me for (three words; not *not a problem* or *no big deal*)

entries.related: *No problem* — casual, very common; *My pleasure* — warm: I was happy to do it; *Anytime* — I'd gladly do it again.

entries.term: it's none of my business, but …
entries.spoken_term: it's none of my business, but
entries.label: softener
entries.meaning: A softener before a personal comment or a piece of advice that you know nobody asked you for.
entries.usage: Said to friends, family and sometimes coworkers before commenting on their relationship, money, health or choices. It admits that you may be overstepping, but you say it anyway, so it can still sound nosy. *I know it's none of my business, but …* is a common longer form.
examples: **It's none of my business, but** I think you're paying way too much for car insurance.
**I know it's none of my business, but** is everything okay between you and Mike?
My aunt said **it was none of her business, but** I should really see a doctor about that cough.

drill.sentence: {{It's none of my business, but}} are you sure you want to lend your brother that much money?
drill.hint: softener: this personal matter doesn't concern me (not *… pry* or *don't take this the wrong way*)

entries.related: *Not to pry, but …* — similar, before a personal question; *Don't take this the wrong way, but …* — before a comment that could offend; *Mind your own business* — rude: stay out of it.
